title: Clone a huge repository in seconds
summary: Shallow and partial clones both make cloning fast, in completely different ways — and they break different things. Compare them, then repair a CI job that fails because of one.
mental_model: Shallow truncates history: you get the last N commits and nothing before. Partial keeps all commits but skips file contents, fetching them on demand. Shallow breaks history commands; partial only costs you a network round trip.

steps.title: The full clone, for comparison
steps.why: Five commits, a tag, complete history. Everything below is a trade against this baseline.

steps.title: Make a shallow clone
steps.why: `--depth 1` fetches one commit and no ancestors. On a repository with a decade of history this is the difference between four minutes and four seconds — which is why CI systems default to it.
steps.expect: One commit, and a .git/shallow file listing the cut-off point. Note the file:// prefix — a plain local path makes git hardlink the whole object store and ignore --depth entirely.

verify.label: the shallow clone has exactly one commit

steps.title: Watch what breaks
steps.why: No ancestors means no `describe`, no useful `blame`, no `bisect`, and diffs against older commits are impossible. Every CI failure of the form 'fatal: no tag can describe' comes from here.
steps.expect: describe fails, HEAD~2 does not exist, no tags fetched.

steps.title: Deepen or unshallow to repair it
steps.why: `--unshallow` fetches the missing history and removes the shallow marker. `--depth=N` on fetch deepens partially. This is the two-line fix for a CI job that needs `git describe`.
steps.expect: Full history, tags present, describe works, no .git/shallow file.

verify.label: describe works again once tags and history exist
verify.hint: add --tags: unshallowing alone does not fetch them

steps.title: Now a partial clone instead
steps.why: `--filter=blob:none` fetches every commit and tree but no file contents. History commands all work; the files arrive lazily the first time you actually read them.
steps.expect: All five commits and a working describe — unlike the shallow clone.

verify.label: the partial clone has full history

steps.title: See the lazy fetch happen
steps.why: Reading an old file's content triggers a fetch of just that blob. The cost moves from clone time to first-access time, which for CI is usually a much better trade.
steps.expect: The old file content, fetched on demand, and promisor config marking the remote as a lazy source.

steps.title: Choose deliberately
steps.why: For a build that only compiles the tip: shallow is fine and fastest. For anything that reads history — versioning, changelogs, blame annotations, bisect — partial is the correct choice.
commands: sh -c 'echo shallow: $(cd ../shallow && git log --oneline | wc -l) commits'
sh -c 'echo partial: $(cd ../partial && git log --oneline | wc -l) commits'
steps.expect: Both now usable, having got there very differently.

verify.label: the shallow clone was repaired with --unshallow
the partial clone had full history from the start
…and is configured to fetch blobs lazily

pitfalls: `git fetch --unshallow` does not fetch tags. Add `--tags`, or `git describe` still fails.
A shallow clone cannot be pushed from in some server configurations, and `git bisect` is useless in one.
Partial clones need a server that supports the protocol. GitHub, GitLab and modern Gitea do; some older self-hosted setups do not.
In CI, `actions/checkout` defaults to depth 1. Set `fetch-depth: 0` when your build reads history — that single line fixes most versioning failures.
cheatsheet: partial: all history, no file contents yet
